# Contributing

We love contributors! Pact-js is maintained and contributed to by developers just like you.

We have a development channel in the pact-foundation [slack] (`#pact-js-development`).

## Raising issues

Before raising an issue, make sure you have checked the open and closed issues to see if an answer is provided there.
There may also be an answer to your question on [stackoverflow].

Please provide the following information with your issue to enable us to respond as quickly as possible.

- The relevant versions of the packages you are using.
- The steps to recreate your issue.
- An executable code example where possible. You can fork this repository and use one of the [examples] to quickly recreate your issue.

## Key Branches

* `master` - this is the current main version supporting the 11.x.x release line. Most investment will be here, including major new features, enhancements, bug fixes, security patches, etc.
* `9.x.x` - this is the previous major version supporting the 9.x.x release line. Critical security patches and bug fixes will be provided as a priority.
* There is no tracking or release branch for 10.x.x at this stage. Most users can be encouraged to jump straight to 11.x.x noting the single breaking change (see the migration guide).

## I want to contribute code but don't know where to start

If you're not sure where to start, look for the [help wanted](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-js/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22help+wanted%22)
label in our issue tracker. If you have an idea that you think would be great, come and chat to us on [slack] in the `#pact-js` channel, or open a feature request issue.

## I'm ready to contribute code

Awesome! We have some guidelines here that will help your PR be accepted:

### Commit messages

Pact JS uses the [Conventional Changelog](https://github.com/bcoe/conventional-changelog-standard/blob/master/convention.md)
commit message conventions. Please ensure you follow the guidelines, as they
help us automate our release process.

You can take a look at the git history (`git log`) to get the gist of it.
If you have questions, feel free to reach out in `#pact-js` in our [slack
community](https://pact-foundation.slack.com/).

If you'd like to get some CLI assistance, getting setup is easy:

```shell
npm install commitizen -g
npm i -g cz-conventional-changelog
```

`git cz` to commit and commitizen will guide you.

#### Release notes

Commit messages with `fix` or `feat` prefixes will appear in the release notes. 
These communicate changes that users may want to know about.

* `feat(<scope>):` or `feat:` messages appear under "New Features", and trigger minor version bumps.
* `fix(<scope>):` or `fix:` messages appear under "Fixes and improvements", and trigger patch version bumps.

If your commit message introduces a breaking change, please include a footer that starts with `BREAKING CHANGE:`.
For more information, please see the [Conventional Changelog](https://github.com/bcoe/conventional-changelog-standard/blob/master/convention.md)
guidelines.

(Also, if you are committing breaking changes, you may want to check with the other maintainers on slack first).

Examples of `fix` include bug fixes and dependency bumps that users of pact-js may want to know about.

Examples of `feat` include new features and substantial modifications to existing features.

Examples of things that we'd prefer not to appear in the release notes include documentation updates, 
modified or new examples, refactorings, new tests, etc. We usually use one of `chore`, `style`, 
`refactor`, or `test` as appropriate.

## Code style and formatting

We use [Biome](https://biomejs.dev/) for both formatting and linting.

The recommended approach is to install the [Biome VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=biomejs.biome) and configure it to format on save 👌. If not, don't worry, our lint step will catch it.

## Pull requests

- Please write tests for any changes.
- Please follow existing code style and conventions.
- Please separate unrelated changes into multiple pull requests.
- For bigger changes, make sure you start a discussion first by creating an issue and explaining the intended change.

# Consumer Tests

## Contract Testing Process (HTTP)

Pact is a consumer-driven contract testing tool, which is a fancy way of saying that the API `Consumer` writes a test to set out its assumptions and needs of its API `Provider`(s). By unit testing our API client with Pact, it will produce a `contract` that we can share to our `Provider` to confirm these assumptions and prevent breaking changes.

The process looks like this:

![diagram](./diagrams/summary.png)

1. The consumer writes a unit test of its behaviour using a Mock provided by Pact
1. Pact writes the interactions into a contract file (as a JSON document)
1. The consumer publishes the contract to a broker (or shares the file in some other way)
1. Pact retrieves the contracts and replays the requests against a locally running provider
1. The provider should stub out its dependencies during a Pact test, to ensure tests are fast and more deterministic.

In this document, we will cover steps 1-3.

## Consumer package

To use the library on your tests, add the pact dependency:

```javascript
const { Pact } = require("@pact-foundation/pact")
```

`PactV4` aliased as `Pact` is the latest version of this library, supporting up to and including version 4 of the [Pact Specification](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-specification/). It also allows interactions of multiple types (HTTP, async, synchronous). For previous versions, see below.

<details>

<summary>Previous versions</summary>


```javascript
const { PactV2 } = require("@pact-foundation/pact")   // Supports up to and including Pact Specification version 2
const { PactV3 } = require("@pact-foundation/pact") // Supports up to and including Pact Specification version 3
```

You should use the `Pact` interface unless you can't, and set the specification version via `spec` to the desired serialisation format.

</details>

The `Pact` class provides the following high-level APIs, they are listed in the order in which they typically get called in the lifecycle of testing a consumer:

### API

<details>

<summary>Consumer API</summary>

The Pact SDK uses a fluent builder to create interactions.

| API                              | Options                            | Description                                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `new Pact(options)`              | See constructor options below      | Creates a Mock Server test double of your Provider API. The class is **not** thread safe, but you can run tests in parallel by creating as many instances as you need. |
| `addInteraction(...)`            | `V4UnconfiguredInteraction`        | Start a builder for an HTTP interaction                                                                                                                                |
| `addSynchronousInteraction(...)` | `V4UnconfiguredSynchronousMessage` | Start a builder for an asynchronous message                                                                                                                            |

_NOTE:_ V4 also supports interaction metadata for advanced workflows using `pending(...)`, `comment(...)`, and `testName(...)`. See [Interaction metadata (V4, advanced)](#interaction-metadata-v4-advanced).

#### Common methods to builders


| `given(...)`                           | Object             | Set one or more provider states for the interaction                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `uponReceiving(...)`                   | string                        | The scenario name. The combination of `given` and `uponReceiving` must be unique in the pact file                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `executeTest(...)`                     | -                             | Executes a user defined function, passing in details of the dynamic mock service for use in the test. If successful, the pact file is updated. The function signature changes depending on the setup and context of the interaction.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

</details>

<details>

<summary>Constructor</summary>

| Parameter  | Required? | Type    | Description                                                                               |
| ---------- | --------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `consumer` | yes       | string  | The name of the consumer                                                                  |
| `provider` | yes       | string  | The name of the provider                                                                  |
| `port`     | no        | number  | The port to run the mock service on, defaults to a random machine assigned available port |
| `host`     | no        | string  | The host to run the mock service, defaults to 127.0.0.1                                   |
| `tls`      | no        | boolean | flag to identify which protocol to be used (default false, HTTP)                          |
| `cors`     | no        | boolean | Allow CORS preflight requests to be handled by the mock server (default true)             |
| `dir`      | no        | string  | Directory to output pact files                                                            |
| `log`      | no        | string  | File to log to                                                                            |
| `logLevel` | no        | string  | Log level: one of 'trace', 'debug', 'info', 'error', 'fatal' or 'warn'                    |
| `spec`     | no        | number  | Pact specification version (defaults to 2)                                                |

</details>

### Example

The first step is to create a test for your API Consumer. The example below uses [Mocha](https://mochajs.org), and demonstrates the basic approach:

1.  Create the Pact object
1.  Start the Mock Provider that will stand in for your actual Provider
1.  Add the interactions you expect your consumer code to make when executing the tests
1.  Write your tests - the important thing here is that you test the outbound _collaborating_ function which calls the Provider, and not just issue raw http requests to the Provider. This ensures you are testing your actual running code, just like you would in any other unit test, and that the tests will always remain up to date with what your consumer is doing.
1.  Validate the expected interactions were made between your consumer and the Mock Service
1.  Generate the pact(s)

_NOTE: you must also ensure you clear out your pact directory prior to running tests to ensure outdated interactions do not hang around_

Check out the [examples](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-js/tree/master/examples/) for more of these.

# Migrating from 15.x.x to 16.x.x

## New features

1. **GraphQL support for V3 and V4 interfaces** — GraphQL interactions can now be used with `PactV3` and `PactV4` (fixes [#1093](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-js/issues/1093))
2. **Asynchronous message support** — V4 now supports asynchronous messages via `addAsynchronousInteraction()` (fixes [#1186](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-js/issues/1186))
3. **Synchronous message bodies** — Bodies are now passed into the `executeTest` function for synchronous messages
4. **Matching rules support** — `withMatchingRules` is now available for HTTP, async, and sync interactions

## Breaking changes

### Import renames

The default `Pact` and `Matchers` exports have been changed to point to the V4 and V3 implementations respectively. The previous V2 implementations are still available under explicit names:

| v15 export   | v16 export         | Notes                               |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `Pact`       | `PactV2`           | The V2 HTTP Pact DSL                |
| `Matchers`   | `MatchersV2`       | The V2 matchers                     |
| `PactV4`     | `Pact` (alias)     | The V4 Pact DSL is now the default  |
| `MatchersV3` | `Matchers` (alias) | The V3 matchers are now the default |

> **Note**: `PactV3` and `MatchersV3` continue to be available as named exports — they are unchanged.

### Node.js version

Node.js **>=20** is now required. Versions 16–19 are no longer supported as they have reached end-of-life. If you cannot upgrade Node.js, remain on pact-js v15.

### Downstream packages

The import renames above are known to impact packages that re-export or depend on the `Pact` / `Matchers` types:

- [`jest-pact`](https://github.com/pact-foundation/jest-pact)
- [`nestjs-pact`](https://github.com/pact-foundation/nestjs-pact)

Check for updated versions of these packages that are compatible with pact-js v16.

## Migration guide

### Consumer

#### Quick reference

| If you currently import… | Action                                                     |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Pact` (V2 DSL)          | Rename to `PactV2` — **required**                          |
| `Matchers` (V2 matchers) | Rename to `MatchersV2` — **required**                      |
| `PactV4`                 | Can be simplified to `Pact` — optional but recommended     |
| `MatchersV3`             | Can be simplified to `Matchers` — optional but recommended |
| `PactV3`                 | No changes needed                                          |

#### Upgrading to the V4 DSL (recommended)

If your imports already use the V4 interface:

```js
import {
  SpecificationVersion,
  PactV4,
  LogLevel,
  MatchersV3,
} from '@pact-foundation/pact';
```

Simplify to:

```js
import {
  SpecificationVersion,
  Pact,
  LogLevel,
  Matchers,
} from '@pact-foundation/pact';
```

No other code changes are needed — the API is identical.

#### Preserving V2 behaviour

If your imports use the V2 interface and you want to keep using it, you need to update the import names.

**CommonJS:**

```js
// Before
const { Pact, Matchers } = require('@pact-foundation/pact');

// After
const { PactV2: Pact, MatchersV2: Matchers } = require('@pact-foundation/pact');
```

**ES Modules:**

```js
// Before
import {
  Pact,
  GraphQLInteraction,
  Matchers,
  LogLevel,
} from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// After
import {
  PactV2 as Pact,
  GraphQLInteraction,
  MatchersV2 as Matchers,
  LogLevel,
} from '@pact-foundation/pact';
```

### Provider

No changes are required for provider verification — the `Verifier` API is fully backwards compatible.

# Provider Verification

Pact JS supports both HTTP and non-HTTP verification (using plugins).

## Contract Testing Process (HTTP)

Pact is a consumer-driven contract testing tool, which is a fancy way of saying that the API `Consumer` writes a test to set out its assumptions and needs of its API `Provider`(s). By unit testing our API client with Pact, it will produce a `contract` that we can share to our `Provider` to confirm these assumptions and prevent breaking changes.

The process looks like this:

![diagram](./diagrams/summary.png)

1. The consumer writes a unit test of its behaviour using a Mock provided by Pact
1. Pact writes the interactions into a contract file (as a JSON document)
1. The consumer publishes the contract to a broker (or shares the file in some other way)
1. Pact retrieves the contracts and replays the requests against a locally running provider
1. The provider should stub out its dependencies during a Pact test, to ensure tests are fast and more deterministic.

In this document, we will cover steps 4-5.

## HTTP Provider package

The provider interface is: `Verifier`.

### Provider API Testing

<details>

<summary>Provider API</summary>

Once you have created Pacts for your Consumer, you need to validate those Pacts against your Provider. The Verifier object provides the following API for you to do so:

| API                |  Options  | Returns   | Description           |
| ------------------ | :-------: | --------- | --------------------- |
| `verifyProvider()` | See below | `Promise` | Start the Mock Server |

</details>

1.  Start your local Provider service.
1.  Optionally, instrument your API with ability to configure [provider states](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-provider-verifier/)
1.  Then run the Provider side verification step

```js
const { Verifier } = require('@pact-foundation/pact');
const opts = {
  ...
};

new Verifier(opts).verifyProvider().then(function () {
	// do something
});
```

# Troubleshooting

If you are having issues, a good place to start is setting `logLevel: 'debug'` when configuring the `new Pact({...})` object. This will give you detailed in/out requests as far as Pact sees them during verification.

## Corporate Proxies / Firewalls

If you're on a corporate machine, it's common for all network calls to route through a proxy - even requests that go to your own machine!

The symptom presents as follows:

1. The mock server starts up correctly, as shown by a debug level log message such as this:

   ```
   [2021-11-22 11:16:01.214 +0000] DEBUG (3863 on Matts-iMac): pact-core@11.0.1: INFO  WEBrick::HTTPServer#start: pid=3864 port=50337
   ```

2. You receive a conflicting message such as "The pact mock service doesn't appear to be running" and the tests never run or any before all blocks fail to complete.

The problem is that the Pact framework attempts to ensure the mock service can be communicated with before the tests run. It does so via an HTTP call, which will be sent via any intermediate proxies if configured. The proxy is unlikely to know how send the request back to your machine, which results in a timeout or error.

This may be resolved by ensuring the `http_proxy`, `https_proxy` and `no_proxy` directives are correctly set (usually, by excluding the address of the mock server such as `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`).

## Alpine + Docker

Alpine is not currently supported, you should run your Pact tests in a full linux distribution such as Ubuntu or Debian.
As a workaround to prevent Docker build failure you may install the following packages:
```sh
RUN apk add --no-cache libc6-compat python3 make g++
```

## Test fails when it should pass

TL;DR - you almost certainly have not properly handled (returned) a Promise.

We see this sort of thing all of the time:

```js
it("returns a successful thing", () => {
  executeApiCallThatIsAPromise()
    .then((response) => {
      expect(response.data).to.eq({...})
    })
    .then(() => {
      provider.verify()
    })
  })
```

There are several problems with this:

1. in the "returns a successful thing", the call to `executeApiCallThatIsAPromise()` is a function that returns a Promise, but is not returned by the function (`it` block) - this leaves a dangling, unhandled Promise. In your case it fails, but by the time it does the `it` block has already completed without problems - and returns a green result ✅.
1. In the `then` block, the call to `provider.verify()` is also not returned, and will suffer the same fate as (1)

_Side note_: Jasmine and other test frameworks may detect an unhandled promise rejection and report on it.

The correct code for the above is:

```js
it("returns a successful thing", () => {
  return executeApiCallThatIsAPromise() // <- explicit return here, you could also use the "async/await" syntax here
    .then((response) => {
      expect(response.data).to.eq({...})
    })
    .then(() => provider.verify()) // provider.verify() also returned
  })
```

## Test intermittent failures

See above - you probably have not returned a Promise when you should have.

## Re-run specific verification failures

If you prefix your test command (e.g. `npm t`) with the following environment variables, you can selectively run a specific interaction during provider verification.

| variable name          | description                                                                                            | comments    |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| PACT_DESCRIPTION       | select all tests that contain this string in its `description`(from the test output, or the pact file) |             |
| PACT_PROVIDER_STATE    | select all tests that contain this string in on of its `providerState`                                 |             |
| PACT_PROVIDER_NO_STATE | set to `TRUE` to select all tests what don't have any `providerState`                                  | only for V3 |

For the e2e example, let's assume we have the following failure:

```sh
3 interactions, 2 failures

Failed interactions:

* A request for all animals given Has some animals

* A request for an animal with id 1 given Has an animal with ID 1
```

If we wanted to target the second failure, we can extract the description and state as the bits before and after the word "given":

```sh
PACT_DESCRIPTION="A request for an animal with ID 1" PACT_PROVIDER_STATE="Has an animal with ID 1" npm t
```

## Usage with Jest

TL;DR - consider the use of `jest-pact` package.

Jest uses JSDOM under the hood which may cause issues with libraries making HTTP request.

You'll need to add the following snippet to your `package.json` to ensure it uses
the proper Node environment:

```js
"jest": {
  "testEnvironment": "node"
}
```

Also, [from Jest 20](https://facebook.github.io/jest/blog/2017/05/06/jest-20-delightful-testing-multi-project-runner.html), you can add the environment to the top of the test file as a comment. This will allow your pact test to run along side the rest of your JSDOM env tests.

```js
/**
 * @jest-environment node
 */
```

Jest also runs tests in parallel by default, which can be problematic with Pact which is stateful. See [parallel tests](#parallel-tests) to see how to make it run in parallel, or run Jest with the `--runInBand` [option](https://facebook.github.io/jest/docs/en/cli.html#runinband) to run them sequentially.

See [this issue](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-js/issues/10) for background.

## Usage with Angular

You way want to consider using this starter schematic: https://github.com/niklas-wortmann/ngx-pact

Angular's HttpClient filters out many headers from the response object, this may cause issues when validating a response in tests.

You'll need to add the additional header `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, this will allow specified headers to be passed to the response object. This can be done by declaring the header in the `willRespondWith` section of your interaction:

```js
"willRespondWith": {
  "headers": {
    "Access-Control-Expose-Headers": like("My-Header"),
    "My-Header": "..."
  },
  ...
}
```

## Using Pact in non-Node environments such as Karma

Pact requires a Node runtime to be able to start and stop Mock servers, write logs and other things.

However, when used within browser or non-Node based environments - such as with Karma or ng-test - this is not possible.

You will need a Node based test framework such as Jest or Mocha.

## Unable to run tests in Alpine linux

Alpine linux is currently [not supported](https://github.com/pact-foundation/pact-net/issues/387).

## How do I test negative scenarios, such as an HTTP `400`, `401` or `500`?

Testing HTTP errors is straightforward with Pact, however most api clients (such as Axios) will throw if they receive a response code `>= 400`. It might not be obvious that you need to modify your test slightly to deal with this.

Take this example where we would like to test a `400`:

```js
it('should return an error when an invalid ID is requested', async () => {
    await provider.addInteraction({
        uponReceiving: 'an invalid request',
        withRequest: {
            method: 'GET',
            path: '/bad/m1xf%d5/path/'
        },
        willRespondWith: {
            status: 400,
            body: {
                error: 'BadRequest',
                message: 'Invalid ID format',
                statusCode: 400
            }
        }
    });

    const api = new ApiClient(provider.mockService.baseUrl);
    const response = await api().doSomething('m1xf%d5'); // <-- throws
    expect(response).toThrow('400: Bad Request');        // <-- Too late, already thrown!
});
```

This test will fail, because the use of `await` will throw if the promise is rejected.

To correct this test, you should pass the Promise to `expect` directly, and `return` or `await` the result.

For example, with Jest you could do this:

```js
await expect(api.doSomething('m1xf%d5')).rejects.toMatch('400: Bad Request');
```

report.overview: Pact JS is a TypeScript contract-testing SDK for teams building HTTP APIs and message-based integrations. Consumer tests define expected interactions, exercise application clients or message handlers, and generate pact files; provider verification checks those contracts against running services or registered message producers. Its distinctive architecture combines versioned JavaScript builders with native pact-core operations, an Express verification proxy, flexible matching rules, and plugins for additional content types and transports.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to pact-js at commit 18f30a1aa44a948b3249a72879da3cff26c42d12. Treat this brief as a bounded source investigation, not exhaustive coverage or evidence of passing tests. Tests and CI configuration were inspected, not executed. Preserve the task's read-only restrictions unless a subsequent instruction explicitly changes scope: inspect public tracked source, prefix shell commands with rtk proxy, and do not execute repository code, install dependencies, invoke network tools, or read credentials and environment files.

Start with package.json, src/index.ts, src/v4/index.ts, tsconfig.json, vitest.config.ts, and the smallest implementation and test files relevant to the requested change. The package is @pact-foundation/pact 17.1.4 and requires Node >=22. Historical documentation and example manifests contain older Node requirements. The default Pact export aliases PactV4; Matchers aliases MatchersV3. PactV2, PactV3, and older message APIs remain public compatibility surfaces.

Understand the native boundary before changing behavior. makeConsumerPact creates pact-core handles; JavaScript builders configure interactions through those handles. Native core supplies mock-server matching, contract serialization, verification, and plugin operations. This checkout does not establish the dependency's internal implementation. V4 factory methods create staged builders and pass a cleanup callback that recreates the parent pact handle.

Trace HTTP consumer work through PactV4.addInteraction, UnconfiguredInteraction.withRequest, RequestBuilder, InteractionWithRequest.willRespondWith, ResponseBuilder, and the shared HTTP executeTest function. The callback receives the mock URL and port. Callback errors and mismatch results determine failure; the normal successful path writes the pact, cleans the mock server and plugins, and resets the parent. Read the experimental mismatch filter before interpreting failure branches.

Trace provider work through Verifier.verifyProvider, createProxy, waitForServerReady, runProviderVerification, and serviceFactory.verifyPacts. The proxy handles /_pactSetup and /_messages before forwarding other traffic. State handlers are keyed by state strings; message providers by interaction descriptions. Hooks record failures for later rejection, while ordinary state-handler exceptions are logged and answered with HTTP 200. Request filters apply before endpoint dispatch. TLS credentials stay in the proxy target rather than being forwarded to core.

For messaging, distinguish V4 asynchronous contents.content from legacy contents and synchronous Request/Response envelopes. Nontransport callbacks receive generated messages directly; plugin transports use native mock servers. Keep matcher declarations distinct from reified example values.

When execution becomes authorized, select the smallest relevant Vitest spec first, then appropriate consumer/provider examples or regression suites. Root npm test invokes a pretest installer that downloads binaries, writes under ~/.pact, and executes the plugin CLI. Regression npm test cleans pact outputs and runs consumers before providers. Formatting uses Biome and type checking uses tsc --noEmit. Preserve public types and exports, include tests for meaningful behavioral changes, and report actual results separately from source observations. Review cleanup, logging, proxy reconstruction, and compatibility branches carefully; do not characterize source hypotheses as confirmed vulnerabilities.

system_map.summary: The repository delivers an npm SDK whose public entrypoint exposes several generations of contract-testing APIs. JavaScript owns builder state, callbacks, and verification middleware, while pact-core owns native contract and mock-server operations. Generated pact files connect consumer and provider testing; release and documentation workflows distribute the package and synchronize documentation.

claims.claim: src/index.ts exports PactV2, Verifier, legacy message APIs, V3 exports, and V4 exports; PactV4 is aliased as Pact and MatchersV3 as Matchers.
PactV3 and PactV4 create ConsumerPact handles through makeConsumerPact and attach pact-js version metadata; their default specification versions are V3 and V4 respectively.

The API generations use different orchestration structures: V2 exposes setup/addInteraction/verify, V3 owns a mutable current interaction, and V4 returns staged HTTP, synchronous, asynchronous, and GraphQL builders.
Provider verification creates a temporary Express/http-proxy server with state and message endpoints, then passes its address and a message transport to serviceFactory.verifyPacts.
Contract persistence is delegated to pact-core writePactFile calls using caller-selected directories or ./pacts; V2 additionally passes merge-versus-overwrite behavior.

VerifierOptions combines pact-core options with local ProxyOptions; documented broker integration includes pactBrokerUrl, consumerVersionSelectors, broker authentication, and publishVerificationResult.

package.json requires Node >=22 and defines npm scripts for tsc compilation/distribution, Biome formatting/linting, tsc --noEmit, Vitest, and regression testing; tsconfig emits declarations and source maps into dist.
Publishing is dispatch-driven: latest checks out master and runs release.sh with SKIP_EXAMPLES=true, while the 9.x workflow checks out 9.x.x; Markdown pushes on master dispatch a docs.pact.io update.

feature_catalog.summary: The public surface supports HTTP request/response contracts, asynchronous event contracts, synchronous messages, and GraphQL over HTTP. Matching APIs express flexible contracts while supplying concrete examples to consumer tests. Provider callbacks, broker options, interaction metadata, and plugins support more involved verification workflows.

claims.claim: V4 HTTP tests configure method/path, query parameters, headers, body, and expected status through fluent builders, then execute a callback against a dynamic mock server with configurable host, port, TLS, and CORS.
MatchersV3 supplies type, regex, numeric, bounded-array, key/value, status-code, date/time, UUID, URL, equality, inclusion, null, and array-containing declarations.

HTTP builders accept binary files, Buffer bodies, multipart files with an optional boundary, and explicit matching rules; XmlBuilder and XmlElement construct XML templates containing text and repeated-element matchers.
addGraphQLInteraction supports operation names, variables, queries, and mutations; query text is validated and wrapped in a whitespace-flexible regex inside an application/json request body.

V4 asynchronous messages support JSON or binary content, metadata, and explicit rules; synchronous messages separately configure request and response content and expose Request plus a Response array to callbacks.

Provider verification supports named state setup/teardown handlers, beforeEach/afterEach hooks, Express request filters, message producer registries, TLS client credentials, and optional broker result publication.

given accepts state parameters, fromProviderState declares generator expressions, and provider callbacks can return generated values; the account example connects ${accountId} to the handler's returned accountId.
HTTP and message builders support pending flags, comments, test names, and grouped references; usingPlugin loads named/versioned plugins, and message plugin builders can start custom transports.

data_flow.summary: Consumer inputs become native interaction declarations rather than a JavaScript implementation of contract matching. Native mock servers or reified messages feed application callbacks, and successful orchestration writes contracts to disk. Provider verification routes native requests through JavaScript middleware, state callbacks, and message producers before returning results to the caller.

claims.claim: matcherValueOrString preserves string inputs and JSON-stringifies other values; RequestBuilder translates query/header arrays into indexed native withQuery/withRequestHeader calls and serializes JSON bodies.
Status matchers split into a concrete example passed to withStatus and status matching rules passed to withResponseMatchingRules; ordinary matcher reification recursively extracts examples.

Explicit Rules inputs are checked for recognized parts and rule-array/path structure, then converted to part/path/matchers maps; conversion removes pact:generator:type and emits entries only for truthy rule.path.
V4 HTTP executeTest captures callback errors, reads native mismatches and match success, and on its normal success branch writes a pact before mock-server cleanup, plugin cleanup, and parent reset.

Asynchronous reification parses native JSON into contents.content plus metadata and base64-decodes content when the builder marked it binary; synchronous callbacks receive native request and response contents directly.

Provider-state POST bodies become ProviderState values; setupStates selects stateHandlers[state.state], invokes setup or teardown with params, and returns callback data as JSON for native verification.

The verification proxy parses JSON, form, and raw bodies before requestFilter; forwarding reconstructs Buffers or JSON objects into a readable body stream and uses providerBaseUrl, TLS options, and HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY.

/_messages dispatches by description, copies request metadata, decodes encoded synchronous content, and invokes the producer; metadata-bearing outputs become base64 JSON headers plus a content-type-aware response, while errors return HTTP 500.

behavior_traces.summary: Three concrete flows were followed through source: V4 HTTP consumer testing, HTTP provider verification, and V4 asynchronous message testing. Each trace follows declaration, execution, and persistence or result handling. The examples show application clients and handlers participating in those flows rather than treating the library's builders as the entire test.

claims.claim: HTTP consumer startup: new Pact constructs PactV4 → setup → makeConsumerPact with default V4 → addMetadata; addInteraction then creates a native interaction and an UnconfiguredInteraction carrying a parent-reset callback.

HTTP declaration: given/uponReceiving configure native state and description → withRequest configures method/path and runs RequestBuilder → willRespondWith sets status and runs ResponseBuilder → returns InteractionWithResponse.

HTTP execution: InteractionWithResponse.executeTest → shared executeTest → native transport mock startup → UserServiceClient.getUser sends Axios GET → callback assertions → mismatch checks → writePactFile/cleanup/reset; callback errors are rethrown and failure branches skip writing.

Provider startup: the example starts createApp on port 3001 → constructs Verifier with the generated pact path and state handlers → verifyProvider creates hooks state and proxy → waitForServerReady → runProviderVerification → verifyPacts.

Provider state and request replay: /_pactSetup runs hook middleware before requestFilter and state dispatch → setupStates invokes the named callback → clearUsers/seedUser populate the example Map → other requests reach proxy.web → createApp returns /users or /users/:id JSON.

Provider completion: registerHooks records hook exceptions while continuing middleware; after verifyPacts resolves, verifyProvider closes the server and rejects recorded hook errors, and its catch branch also closes the server before rethrowing.

Async message declaration: PactV4.addAsynchronousInteraction → newAsynchronousMessage → given → expectsToReceive → AsynchronousMessageBuilder.withJSONContent/withMetadata; the OrderPlaced example supplies matching declarations and queue metadata.

Async execution and persistence: AsynchronousMessageWithContent.executeTest → executeNonTransportTest → reifyMessage/JSON.parse → v4SynchronousBodyHandler extracts contents.content → application handler; callback failure cleans without writing, while success writes ./pacts or opts.dir, cleans plugins, and resets.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; their existence establishes intended checks rather than passing results. Root Vitest combines mocked unit tests with native-backed integration tests, while examples and regression packages run consumer suites before provider suites. This is a bounded inspection, and the selected lifecycle specs do not establish coverage of every mismatch, persistence, transport, or cleanup failure branch.

claims.claim: Root npm test maps to vitest run with a plugin-installing pretest; Vitest discovers src/**/*.spec.ts, uses forks and 60-second timeouts, writes JUnit output, and configures V8 coverage with 50% line/statement thresholds.

The inspected V3 and V4 HTTP lifecycle specs replace ConsumerPact operations with mocks and assert CORS, HTTP/HTTPS selection, and a negative startup result; those files do not test mismatch rejection or write/cleanup exceptions.

hooks.spec.ts drives synthetic setup/teardown requests to test once-per-interaction execution, multiple states, subsequent interactions after hook failure, continued next(), and retried setup idempotence.

Verifier tests mock the proxy and check closure on resolution/rejection plus exclusion of TLS credentials from core options; proxyRequest tests inspect target credentials, SSL/origin options, proxy-env precedence, and readable buffers, without establishing a real mTLS handshake.
pact.integration.spec.ts uses actual Axios and TCP interactions, reads generated pact JSON to assert metadata/references, and exercises the MATT plugin over HTTP and synchronous TCP.

Regression configs explicitly enumerate consumer/provider files and alias the SDK to src/index.ts; provider configuration substitutes an aws-sdk mock and inlines graphql-http, while the package runs consumers before providers after cleaning pact outputs.

Example suites cover application-client HTTP calls, GraphQL query requests, message handling/production, and provider-generated IDs; their manifests separate consumer and provider commands and order them in npm test.

Test CI defines Node 22/24/26 across macOS, Linux x64/ARM, and Windows, plus Alpine, lint, format, examples, and regression jobs; the completion job rejects failed, cancelled, or skipped dependencies and unit jobs upload coverage/test reports.

risk_map.summary: These findings are source observations and explicitly labeled hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Sensitive boundaries include temporary HTTP listeners, request logging, caller-selected filesystem paths, and plugin executables installed outside the checkout. Failure handling deserves particular attention because ordinary state errors, experimental mismatch filtering, and cleanup exceptions follow different paths.

claims.claim: State-handler exceptions are logged and answered with HTTP 200, unlike hook exceptions accumulated for final rejection; stateHandler.spec.ts explicitly asserts this successful HTTP response after a rejected setup callback.

Hypothesis: debug/trace output can expose sensitive test data because request/response tracers include bodies and headers and verifier trace logging serializes core options, which may contain broker authentication fields.

Hypothesis: legacy MessageProviderPact may expose its callback dispatcher beyond loopback because setupProxyServer calls listen() without a host and registers a catch-all handler; the modern verifier explicitly defaults its bind host to 127.0.0.1.

Filesystem/process boundaries are caller-sensitive: binaryFile reads the supplied path without repo-root restriction, pact output uses opts.dir, and root pretest downloads a CLI into ~/.pact/bin then executes it to install MATT; the inspected downloader contains no checksum-validation step.

Any nonempty PACT_EXPERIMENTAL_FEATURE_ALLOW_MISSING_REQUESTS value activates filtering that removes plugin mismatch objects and request-mismatch entries; HTTP execution rejects native failure only when filtered errors remain, so this flag materially changes validation.

Hypothesis: native mismatch inspection or pact-write exceptions can bypass remaining HTTP cleanup because these calls sit outside the callback try/catch and cleanup writes before stopping servers/plugins, without a finally guard.
The public V4UnconfiguredInteraction interface advertises withCompleteRequest, but UnconfiguredInteraction.withCompleteRequest immediately throws an unimplemented error.

Request.send creates an HTTPS agent with rejectUnauthorized=false and maxBodyLength=Infinity for caller-provided URLs; this differs from Verifier's default validateSSL=true, so the helper cannot be assumed to inherit verifier TLS behavior.

extension_points.summary: Extension points are primarily typed builder stages and caller-provided callback registries. Matching declarations and explicit Rules provide two paths into native matching, while plugins add content and transport support. Changes to public capabilities must account for exports, types, concrete builders, and cleanup behavior together.

claims.claim: src/index.ts is the public export aggregation point; V4ConsumerPact factories in PactV4 create HTTP, synchronous, asynchronous, and GraphQL stages and supply their reset callbacks.

HTTP builder callbacks are typed by V4RequestBuilderFunc/V4ResponseBuilderFunc and instantiated as RequestBuilder/ResponseBuilder, making those interfaces and classes the paired extension points for request/response options.

Matcher helpers return declarative objects using pact:matcher:type, value, and optional generator properties; isMatcher and recursive reify define how declarations are recognized and reduced to examples.

Advanced matching plugs in through validateRules/convertRulesToFFI, used by HTTP and message builders; adding a new rule part requires considering validateRules' fixed path/body/header/query/status list.

StateHandlers is a string-keyed registry of promise-returning functions or setup/teardown objects; setupStates performs exact state-name lookup and passes state params to the selected lifecycle function.

messageProviders dispatches by interaction description; providerWithMetadata adapts producers to metadata-bearing responses, while synchronousBodyHandler/asynchronousBodyHandler and their V4 counterparts adapt consumer body functions.
requestFilter is an Express RequestHandler installed before state/message/catch-all dispatch; beforeEach/afterEach hooks are separate setup-path middleware with per-verification HooksState.

usingPlugin calls native addPlugin and switches to plugin-capable stages; RequestWithPluginBuilder extends RequestBuilder with pluginContents, and synchronous plugin startTransport accepts transport/address/config while Verifier appends its message transport.

agent_handoff.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and this inventory is bounded rather than exhaustive. Begin future work at the public export and the specific generation of API being changed, then follow its native calls and lifecycle tests. Preserve compatibility, inspect npm lifecycle side effects before requesting execution, and use source behavior to resolve documentation drift.

claims.claim: Read src/index.ts, src/v4/index.ts, and the migration import table first: unqualified Pact now means V4 and Matchers means V3, while PactV2 preserves the older HTTP interface.

Use the root package's Node >=22 requirement for this checkout; README still describes Node 16+ for v12 and example manifests advertise >=20, so those older statements do not establish current root support.

Formatting conventions are Biome, single-quoted JavaScript, and two-space LF files; npm run check composes format and lint, and lint includes tsc --noEmit. CONTRIBUTING requests tests and separation of unrelated changes.

For later authorized validation, select the affected Vitest spec before broad suites; src/v4/http/index.spec.ts targets transport configuration and hooks.spec.ts targets interaction-boundary behavior. Neither these tests nor configured CI jobs were executed in this investigation.

Inspect lifecycle scripts before execution: root npm test downloads/installs plugins under ~/.pact, regression npm test removes pact directories, and the plugin example's pretest invokes a CLI command whose failure is suppressed with || true.

Preserve consumer-before-provider sequencing: example and regression npm test commands generate contracts first, provider examples read those generated pact paths, and regression configs alias the SDK to local TypeScript source.

Keep message envelopes generation-specific: legacy MessageConsumerPact delivers contents directly, V4 async adapters extract contents.content, and synchronous V4 callbacks expose Request.content plus Response[].content.

Review reset timing when changing synchronous execution: SynchronousMessageWithResponse.executeTest invokes cleanupFn immediately after starting executeNonTransportTest, whose completion cleanup invokes it again; the supplied callback recreates the PactV4 handle.
